name: Oxygen facial
lead: An oxygen facial is a cosmetic skincare treatment in which a handheld wand directs a stream of pressurised, purified oxygen onto the skin together with serums, typically containing hyaluronic acid, vitamins and antioxidants.[1] It is offered for immediate hydration, a plumper look and a "glow", with no downtime.[1]

Grokipedia states that scientific support for the oxygen itself is limited and that dermatologists attribute visible improvements mainly to the serums.[1] No clinical trials of cosmetic oxygen facials were found; the oxygen-related trials that turn up in searches concern medical oxygen therapy.

paras: Treatment typically begins with cleansing and gentle exfoliation, followed by serum application and passes of the oxygen wand, and may end with a mask, moisturiser and sunscreen.[1] Devices are described as delivering roughly 90-95% oxygen.[1]

Grokipedia places the emergence of oxygen facials in the early 2000s, and credits Anthony McMahon with founding Intraceuticals in Australia in 2002, which marketed a "topical hyperbaric oxygen" approach.[1] It reports popularity among celebrities in Hollywood from the mid-2000s.[1]

Providers say the pressurised oxygen improves serum penetration and supports skin cells. Per Grokipedia, how far this overcomes the skin barrier lacks strong scientific support, and the treatment differs from medical hyperbaric oxygen therapy, in which oxygen is breathed in a pressurised chamber.[1]
No studies found. Randomised trials of oxygen delivery in intensive care and surgery exist, but they concern breathing oxygen and are unrelated to cosmetic skin treatment.

timeline.event: Intraceuticals is founded in Australia, per Grokipedia.[1]

card.summary: Pressurised-oxygen facial that infuses serums for an instant glow; no trials of the cosmetic treatment exist.
card.note: Visible effects are attributed by cited sources mainly to the serums; sourcing is thin.

quick.overview:
An oxygen facial blows purified oxygen across the skin while applying serums such as hyaluronic acid. Spas offer it for instant hydration and glow without downtime.

No clinical trials of the cosmetic treatment were found; the one encyclopedia source says evidence for the oxygen itself is limited.
quick.mechanism: A wand delivers a pressurised oxygen stream that is claimed to help serums absorb and support skin; this is not strongly supported scientifically according to the source.
quick.risks: No adverse-event data were found. It is described as non-invasive with no downtime, and is distinct from medical hyperbaric oxygen therapy.
